knowledge_point.title: Calculating Flux Across a Square Using Symmetry

question.:question/worked-solution:
The outward flux is

$$
\Phi=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
=\sum_{k=1}^{4}\int_{C_k}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_k\,\mathrm ds.
$$

![Sides and outward normals](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179646/cdf46d05554fc51e0cbbc472b1dcc889b629195112d8faaea6789f38e2231823-solution.png)

The right, top, left and bottom sides have outward unit normals $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$, $-\mathbf i$ and $-\mathbf j$, respectively.

The uniform field is parallel to the top and bottom sides, so their normal components are zero. On the right and left sides the normal components are $-4$ and $4$. Each side has length $2$, so the signed contributions cancel:

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi&=(-4)(2)+(4)(2)\\&=0.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating Flux Across a Square Using Symmetry

question.:question/worked-solution:
The outward flux is

$$
\Phi=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
=\sum_{k=1}^{4}\int_{C_k}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_k\,\mathrm ds.
$$

![Sides and outward normals](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179646/5b6ea7d030a2887c8aba898aa32d1f992f7bfdc223812c56199fce3525dbecdf-solution.png)

The right, top, left and bottom sides have outward unit normals $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$, $-\mathbf i$ and $-\mathbf j$, respectively.

The full field does not have equal side fluxes. Decompose it into radial and uniform parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F&=\mathbf R+\mathbf U\\\mathbf R&=(- 2 x)\,\mathbf i+(- 2 y)\,\mathbf j\\\mathbf U&=(-1)\,\mathbf i+(-1)\,\mathbf j.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(\mathbf R+\mathbf U)\cdot\mathbf n=\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf n+\mathbf U\cdot\mathbf n$, the two fluxes add. The uniform part has opposite signed contributions on opposite sides of equal length:

$$
\Phi_{\mathbf U}=(-1)(2)+(-1)(2)-(-1)(2)-(-1)(2)=0.
$$

Now compute the radial part $\mathbf R$. On the right side $C_1$, use $\mathbf r(t)=1\,\mathbf i+t\,\mathbf j$ for $-1\le t\le 1$. Then $\mathbf n_1=\mathbf i$ and $\|\mathbf r\prime(t)\|=1$, so $\mathrm ds=\mathrm dt$. The radial normal component is $-2(1)=-2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi_1&=\int_{-1}^{1}(-2)\,\mathrm dt\\&=(-2)(1-(-1))\\&=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Quarter-turn symmetry preserves both the radial field and the outward normal component, so all four radial contributions are equal. Thus

$$
\Phi_{\mathbf R}=4(-4)=-16.
$$

Adding the uniform part gives $\Phi=-16+0=-16$. As a direct check, the full field gives:

| Side | Normal component | Flux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Right | $-3$ | $-6$ |
| Top | $-3$ | $-6$ |
| Left | $-1$ | $-2$ |
| Bottom | $-1$ | $-2$ |

The four signed contributions sum to $-16$. Only the radial part has four equal contributions.

question.:question/problem:
![Vector field and square](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179646/25100a2bd3f3e750ec66c9f5e035428be21c0a12f199cad95cc17bf4ca36d104-prompt.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F=\left(- \frac{x}{2}\right)\,\mathbf i+\left(- \frac{y}{2}\right)\,\mathbf j$ and the square $C$ with side length $2$, centered at the origin and with sides parallel to the coordinate axes. Calculate the total outward flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$. Enter the exact value.

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*

question.:question/worked-solution:
The outward flux is

$$
\Phi=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
=\sum_{k=1}^{4}\int_{C_k}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_k\,\mathrm ds.
$$

![Sides and outward normals](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179646/25100a2bd3f3e750ec66c9f5e035428be21c0a12f199cad95cc17bf4ca36d104-solution.png)

The right, top, left and bottom sides have outward unit normals $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$, $-\mathbf i$ and $-\mathbf j$, respectively.

On the right side $C_1$, use $\mathbf r(t)=1\,\mathbf i+t\,\mathbf j$ for $-1\le t\le 1$. Then $\mathbf n_1=\mathbf i$ and $\|\mathbf r\prime(t)\|=1$, so $\mathrm ds=\mathrm dt$. The radial normal component is $- \frac{1}{2}(1)=- \frac{1}{2}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi_1&=\int_{-1}^{1}\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)\,\mathrm dt\\&=\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)(1-(-1))\\&=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Quarter-turn symmetry preserves both the radial field and the outward normal component, so all four radial contributions are equal. Thus

$$
\Phi=4(-1)=-4.
$$
